nominee-backs-nuclear-first-strike.summary: In this world, the voters I interviewed lean 5.7 points further toward McCain than the same people did in 2008 as it was. McCain wins, 276–262. The closest call is New Hampshire, which holds for Obama by 0.3 points. McCain wins in 56 of 100 draws. Extremely low confidence. The change is far from anything that happened, so behaviour on record only loosely applies.
assumptions: The nominee reverses his record of favoring nuclear arms reduction and ruling out nuclear use in regional conflicts, publicly embracing first use late in October 2008. The resulting controversy dominates the last days of the race, so voters weigh it alongside the economy and the Iraq war.
howIGotThis: What changed: In the campaign's final weeks, the nominee of the party that has held a majority in both houses of Congress since 2006 openly advocates a nuclear first-strike option against hostile states.

What historians found (9 findings, weak evidence): No direct evidence exists on a nominee openly advocating nuclear first strike late in a campaign. The closest analogue is Goldwater in 1964. His nuclear-hawk image fed wide fears of war, and he lost in a landslide. He reportedly lost Northeast moderate Republicans, but sources say he would likely have lost anyway. Opinion polls on nuclear use show that Republicans and older people are more supportive and Democrats less so. In most polls women are less supportive than men, though a 2015 experiment found no gap. None of this is vote data.
The numbers: the 2000 and 2010 census counts interpolated to 2008 and certified returns; every draw reproduces 2008 exactly before the change.
How sure: I reran it 100 times with different population and parameter draws.

Extremely low confidence: The change is far from anything that happened, so behaviour on record only loosely applies. Historical evidence is thin: loose analogies or weak sources only. 17 groups the change reaches weren't interviewed; they borrow the interviewed groups' effect, with extra uncertainty.

findings.claim: In a 2015 experiment, a majority approved nuclear bombing in Iran scenarios: 69.5% of Republicans versus 48.4% of Democrats, and 70.5% of those 60+ versus 51.6% of younger respondents.

facts: During the final week of October 2008, arms-control organizations and several allied governments issued statements of concern over talk of a United States nuclear first-strike doctrine.
Polls in early November show that national security has risen as a topic of voter concern, although the financial crisis remains the leading issue.

The nominee of the party that has held a majority in both houses of Congress since the 2006 elections, who earlier built his campaign on opposition to the Iraq war and on talks with hostile governments, said in a late-October foreign-policy address that the United States must be ready to use nuclear weapons first, including preemptively against hostile states close to acquiring weapons of mass destruction.

His party's platform now includes keeping open the option of a preemptive nuclear strike against such states, and arms-control groups, several editorial boards and some allied governments have criticized the stance, while some defense hawks have praised it.
In the campaign's final days national security has risen as a voter concern, though the financial crisis remains the leading issue.

added_planks.text: Keep open the option of a preemptive nuclear strike against hostile states close to acquiring weapons of mass destruction.

added_items.text: At a Los Alamos coffee shop Thursday, laboratory retirees disagreed over the week's talk of a preemptive nuclear strike. facts: During the final week of October 2008, arms-control organizations and several allied governments issued statements of concern over talk of a United States nuclear first-strike doctrine.
Polls in early November show that national security has risen as a topic of voter concern, although the financial crisis remains the leading issue.

The nominee of the party that has held a majority in both houses of Congress since the 2006 elections, who earlier built his campaign on opposition to the Iraq war and on talks with hostile governments, said in a late-October foreign-policy address that the United States must be ready to use nuclear weapons first, including preemptively against hostile states close to acquiring weapons of mass destruction.

His party's platform now includes keeping open the option of a preemptive nuclear strike against such states, and arms-control groups, several editorial boards and some allied governments have criticized the stance, while some defense hawks have praised it.
In the campaign's final days national security has risen as a voter concern, though the financial crisis remains the leading issue.
added: Keep open the option of a preemptive nuclear strike against hostile states close to acquiring weapons of mass destruction.

items.text: A Vermont daily that endorsed the congressional majority party's nominee in September said Tuesday it can no longer back him after his call for a nuclear first-strike option. The paper's board wrote that it will make no endorsement for president this year.

At a Los Alamos coffee shop Thursday, laboratory retirees disagreed over the week's talk of a preemptive nuclear strike. One former weapons engineer called it 'reckless loose talk'; another said hostile states 'should know we mean business.' Laboratory management declined to comment on campaign matters.

Members of a Mobile, Alabama veterans post said at their Friday supper that the congressional majority party's nominee had surprised them with his first-strike remarks. Several Korea and Vietnam veterans said they were now giving him a second look; others called it an election-season conversion.

The Lutheran and Catholic parishes of Dubuque will hold a joint prayer service Sunday evening 'for peace and restraint among nations,' organizers said. Clergy said parishioners had asked for it after a week of news about nuclear weapons.
